Pass 2.5 End of Trick 2.5.1 Rule of 8s 2.6 End of Round 3 End of Game 4 2-player variant 5 Room Options 5.1 Game length 5.2 Extra deal in 3-player 5.3 Greater size overwriting 5.4 Permanent Pass Overview [ Fast Tutorial ] Five Three Five is a ladder-climbing game. Your goal is to be the first to get rid of all your cards in hand. A round ends when one player runs out of cards, and all other players gain negative points from the cards left in their hands. When any player has reached -20 points or less, the player with the highest points wins! The game included 65 Weather cards: - Rainy card 1-5 - Cloudy card 7-9 - Sunny card 11-15 Card Uses Player Copies of each card Card Dealt Per Player Undealt Card (left face-down) 2 4 12 x2 (see below) 4 3 4 13 13 4 4 12 4 5 5 12 5 6 5 10 5 Gameplay Beginning from the lead player, players take turns clockwise. On your turn, you must perform 1 of the following 4 actions: Lead , Overwrite , Add , Pass . 1. Lead The first action of the lead player of each trick must always perform this action. Plays any one legal meld type, forming the Central Meld . Legal Meld Types - Singles : A single card - Sets : Two or three cards consisting of identical numbers - Runs : Two or three cards consisting of consecutive numbers 2. Overwrite Play card(s) that are of the same meld type, equal size, and greater strength than the Central Meld . - When playing Singles and Sets: 1s are the lowest strength and 15s are the highest. - When playing Runs: 15s are the lowest strength and 1s are the highest. Note: If the Central Meld contains 4 cards, players cannot take the Overwrite action and must either Add or Pass . 3. Add Play one, two, or three cards to the Central Meld , increasing its overall size . You must make sure after performing an add , the Central Meld must be consecutive numbers or identical numbers. You cannot add a run to a set or add a set to a run. 4. Pass If a player cannot or chooses not to play cards, they pass . Once a player passes, they cannot play any more cards to the trick. End of Trick A trick goes around the table multiple times. The trick ends immediately and the last player to play card(s) wins the trick and will lead the next trick, once any of the following happens: - All but one player passes - All cards of the same number are in the Central Meld - A run of 5 cards is in the Central Meld - An 8 is played using the Rule of 8s Rule of 8s When one or more 8s are used to Overwrite or Add , the trick ends immediately. End of Round As soon as any player runs out of cards, the round ends immediately. Everyone else takes negative points chips equal to the total point value of the cards remaining in their hand. If End of game condition has not been reached, start the next round. The player with the least points is the lead player for the next round. If there is a tie, the lead player is the player closest to the previous round's lead player, clockwise. The points given for cards are as follows: Card 1 2 3 4 5 7 8 9 11 12 13 14 15 Points 3 1 1 1 1 1 5 1 2 2 2 2 3 End of Game If any player reaches -20 or fewer points, the game ends. The player with the highest points is the winner. If there is a tie, the player with the fewest cards left in hand is the winner. 2-player variant When set up, both players are dealt two separate hands of 12 cards: One 12-card-hand for the first half of the round and one 12-card-hand for the second half. Room Options Game length When a player reaches -20 or -10 points, the game ends. For a 2-player game length, you may choose 1 round as well. Extra deal in 3-player Deal 16 cards per player, instead of 12 cards. Greater size overwriting

[Rating: 1/10] Not a bad game, but the results feel more random than usual. Playing a good set can get be stolen away by 1 card, but whatever. There's no such thing as a bad card, even the middles are useful for something, which is maybe more confusing (both for rules and analysis) than it needs to be. And comparing it to similar games, that extra rules weight to make it friendlier and more casual... actually makes me less likely to suggest it.

[Rating: 2/10] Legitimately never got to take a game action past putting cards into hand. Why would anyone play this garbage?

[Rating: 3/10] Played demo game once at Asia Board Game Festival '23.  Card shedding game that just works. Delightfully balanced with the idea of being able to join cards from previous player. Good artwork too. Nice filler game! Works.

[Rating: 4/10] "It's the numbers 1-15 but 6 and 10 are missing" creates exactly the wrong expectations for this game. Actually what you have are three different suits (of lengths 5, 3 and 5). Similarly, saying "runs are stronger the smaller the number" is appealing but wrong. Runs are strongest in the middle suit, because any run in the 3-card suit ends the trick. If it weren't trying to leverage my intuitions from other card games but [i]doing it wrong[/i] this would be a 5.

[Rating: 4/10] It's an okay climbing game, but too often it felt like there were not interesting decisions to be had in how to play a hand out, and instead I was just kind of going through the motions.   It far too often comes to situations where you mostly have to pass because it's hard to get to play your final card or two.   It also struggles because it compares very unfavorably to Scout, which is a great climbing game and is doing several similar ideas, but does them much better.

[Rating: 4/10] Painless way to kill a few minutes, but not much else. Stands in the shadow of far greater climbing games like Scout and Tichu to ever seek out a copy.

[Rating: 4/10] The twist is that you can add to sets (turn a previous player's pair into a triple or quadruple by adding more of that card from your hand).  It's kind of fun.  But I found it added way too much flexibility and made it difficult to make strategic decisions about how to manage your hand.  Occasional opportunities to dump fluke or middling cards and also win the trick/climb creates additional swingyness.
